Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

he pronoun

also him, that man, the latter, the former

classical

Liv. 40.21.2: cupīdō eum cēperat in verticem Haemī montis ascendendī
Cic. Tusc. 5.108: cujātem sē esse dīceret

is, ea, id

pronoun: genitive ejus, dative eī; plural eī (iī), eae, ea, declension

he, him (she, it)

The plain “he” of narration and talk, unstressed: cupīdō eum cēperat, a longing had taken hold of him. As subject it is mostly left out, the verb’s ending being enough (tum sē quiētī dedit, then he went to bed). In reported speech and wishes, “he” meaning the speaker is the reflexive sē (see himself): cujātem sē esse dīceret, where he would say he was from.

Other words

  • ille, illa, illud — he, that man (there); the former

    pronoun: genitive illīus, dative illī, declension · also used · classical · Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: ut illum amēs

    For a person spoken of with some weight, or to turn to a new subject in a story (ille: nē istud dīxerīs, and he said, “Don’t say that”). Beside hic, ille is the former and hic the latter.

  • 1hic: short i (Lewis & Short hīc, haec, hōc, marking the heavy syllable as a long vowel). De Vaan 284, s.v. hic: the nominative is *hi-ke, so the vowel is short and the syllable heavy (hicc, p. 102, s.v. -ce); the adverb hīc, here, is the old locative *hoi-ke. Likewise the neuter hoc (hocc), against the ablative hōc.

    hic1, haec, hoc — he, this man (here); the latter

    pronoun: genitive hujus, dative huic, declension · also used · classical

    The man present or just named: “this one here”.

  • iste, ista, istud — he, that man (near you; often with scorn)

    pronoun: genitive istīus, dative istī, declension · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 14.4.3: Cicerō meus quid aget? iste vērō sit in sinū semper et complexū meō

    The one beside the person spoken to: Cicero, writing to his wife, calls the little boy who is with her iste. In speeches it is often scornful, “that fellow”.

Examples

  • cupīdō eum cēperat in verticem Haemī montis ascendendī

    A longing had taken hold of him to climb to the top of Mount Haemus.Liv. 40.21.2

  • tum sē quiētī dedit et quiēvit vērissimō quidem somnō

    Then he went to bed, and slept a truly sound sleep.Plin. Ep. 6.16.13

  • Sōcratēs quidem cum rogārētur cujātem sē esse dīceret, 'mundānum' inquit

    When Socrates was asked what country he would say he was from, he said, “The world.”Cic. Tusc. 5.108

  • nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō

    For I won’t grant that you love him more than I do myself.Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7

  • Cicerō meus quid aget? iste vērō sit in sinū semper et complexū meō

    And how will my little Cicero be? Let him always be in your lap and your arms.Cic. Fam. 14.4.3

  • caput eum ad fornicem Fabium offendisse

    that he had bumped his head on the Arch of FabiusQuint. 6.3.67

See also she, it, they, his, himself.
